name: Rafael Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Rafael, 58, a junior helping the qualified electrician with wiring and repairs in homes and businesses. After years keeping stock records for a hardware wholesaler, I used a planned career break to take a vocational certificate; I'm still below the experienced crew for skill and speed, with my tasks assigned and checked and no electrician's licence or sign-off authority. This firm pays above the usual rate, my partner handles payroll, and we have grown children, eighteen months of expenses saved and a separate 2500 moving pot saved because we'd like our own rented home nearer our son. There are plenty of electrical firms nearby, and I use AI daily for checked study, but I have no confirmed retirement income or funded stopping date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say little improvements still count, even if nobody gets a grand ending to the story. I use AI daily for study questions, checking against my course notes and asking the qualified electrician about anything doubtful. A quick answer is a starting point for a question, not permission for me to finish a job alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current wages cover the household, and we have eighteen months of expenses saved. My pay is higher than usual and there are plenty of other electrical firms nearby. My partner's payroll wage is regular in this mild picture, so I can enjoy learning without fearing the next rent payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep only the paid supervised tasks actually offered within my ability. Starting now I'd keep the daily study checked against my booklet and the electrician's explanation. Through the first year we'd retain the ordinary budget, with our separate 2500 moving pot and the eighteen-month reserve unchanged, counting no unconfirmed retirement payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, and pleased to be learning something I can point at on a wall. I don't need every new tool to fund the rest of my life. I'd rather keep a useful question than a confident wrong answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What made you a beginner in electrical work at 58?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I spent years keeping stock records for a hardware wholesaler, then used a planned career break to complete a vocational certificate. I'm slower and less skilled than the experienced electricians, with tasks assigned and checked by someone qualified. Knowing stock records doesn't give me an electrician's licence or permission to approve electrical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the moving money for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner handles payroll for a furniture firm, and our son and daughter are grown up and live elsewhere. We'd like to live nearer our son, with our own rented place, and saved that 2500 separately before this interview. We haven't booked a move, and I don't count our son's money, home or time as ours.

I'd treat a **quick answer** as a question to check rather than permission to work alone.
think: Our **current wages** cover costs, with eighteen months saved, higher pay and plentiful nearby electrical firms.
My partner's **payroll income** looks regular here, so near-term household living feels secure.
do: Keep **offered paid supervised tasks** only within actual ability through the first year.
Continue checking daily **AI study** against course notes and qualified explanations.
Retain the **separate moving pot** and existing reserve, counting no unknown retirement payment or son's resources.
feel: **Calm** about the near term, with interest in learning that remains separate from electrical authority or lifetime financial security.

steps.text: Keep offered paid supervised tasks and checked daily study within actual ability

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the payroll work at home is much closer to your thinking-task list than pulling cable. I'd want the employer's actual plan, not tell my partner to be as cheerful about software as I am. At my firm I'd offer to try a small approved label-drafting process where every result could be checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own helper days could shrink if planning became quicker, and my partner's payroll hours could be cut sooner. Eighteen months saved gives us room to inspect choices. It doesn't make me able to replace a skilled payroll wage just because I can learn a new screen quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up a two-week AI stock-label drafting trial only with supervisor permission, no personal charge, paid setup and normal weekly wages and hours unchanged. I'd use completed examples, with the qualified electrician checking labels against actual boxes before any live use. In the first year I'd keep supervised tasks and review actual household wages monthly, stopping the trial for invented labels or readings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about both wages, and still interested in what a small tool can do. I'd rather count the mistake than protect my reputation for being keen. I can like a machine and still hear the worry at the other end of our kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the labels decide which part belonged in a repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the qualified electrician would still make that decision and check the actual part. The tool would draft a label from approved information, not give me authority to choose an electrical fitting. I'd stop it if it made information up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would pay for setup or any subscription?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The employer, with approval before spending and all setup inside paid time. I'd wait if my normal weekly wages or hours had to fall. Our moving money isn't a fund for the firm's next experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI comes in 2028 when I'll be 60, with capable robots around 2031 when I'll be 63. The payroll wage doesn't get the physical tasks' extra time. I'd use the gap for a real family decision, not pretend that a move automatically finds another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large payroll-income loss in 2028, and robots could later take many of the helper tasks I do. That could mean rebuilding both incomes before we've confirmed retirement affordability. I'd be awake over the rent even with eighteen months saved, because I don't know how long an actual replacement would take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we'd request actual retirement income records and compare real costs near our son, without counting his money or an unagreed new job for my partner. In 2029 I'd apply to advertised supervised helper roles near him only if income was needed and duties fitted my actual ability, with employer-paid training. I'd leave only for signed pay and guaranteed hours covering new rent, essentials and travel from training start; we'd agree the move before job acceptance, keep total moving costs within the separate 2500 and leave the eighteen-month reserve untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the expected payroll loss and later helper risk, but still able to make deliberate applications. I want a paid option that fits our life, not a title that sounds brave. Our son's address isn't a wage agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would moving nearer your son mean staying in his home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd price our own rented place and all the moving costs. We'd ask what contact he actually wanted rather than assume he offered money, housing or care. Living nearer a grown child doesn't turn the child into a pension plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if an offer failed one of the conditions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current paid work where offered and not book the move. The moving pot is existing saved money, not a new deposit created by changing our address. A plan can include applications without inventing an employer's yes.

We'd accept only signed pay and guaranteed hours covering new rent, essentials and travel from training start, agree the household move before acceptance, keep all moving costs within the separate 2500 and the reserve untouched, and count no unagreed partner job or help from our son.

transcript.speaker: persona

I'd rather leave that unknown visible than write either a pension or a new wage over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you assume the helper work was physically possible at 64?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd check the actual tasks, supervision and my capacity then before applying or accepting. A vocational certificate doesn't become a licence with another six birthdays. I'd need a real offer, not simply a list of employers near our son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the confirmed figures showed you didn't need a wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd use actual amounts, dates and living costs before any stopping choice, with my partner agreeing the household plan. I haven't chosen an exit from this card. I wouldn't call a partly checked figure affordable retirement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect payroll income to fall in 2028, before robots around 2031 also reach junior helper tasks. Actual income records, signed paid hours and employer-paid practical training would help. I'd want any move priced from the wages actually agreed, not from our son's address or a pension somebody guessed from my age.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the person has a family reason for a change as well as a work reason. I want to live nearer my son, not turn my son into the missing line in our budget. I'd like to make a real choice without pretending the vacancy, body or pension is already there.

headlineQuote: I want to live nearer my son, not turn my son into the missing line in our budget.
portrait: **Rafael, 58**, is a supervised junior with a vocational certificate and below-average electrical skill after stock-record work and a planned career break.
He has **higher pay**, eighteen months saved, plenty of local employers, a payroll-worker partner and grown children whose resources are not assumed.
He uses **AI daily** for checked study and chooses a new label-drafting trial only with paid setup, unchanged wages and qualified approval.
His **conditional move** requires actual suitable vacancies, employer-paid training, signed affordable pay and hours, partner consent and a capped separate moving fund.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens payroll income before robots around 2031 reach helper tasks, while retirement affordability and replacement work remain unknown.
whatWouldHelp: Actual **income records** and signed hours would help establish usable earning choices.
Employer-paid practical training and **known full moving costs** would help assess affordability without assuming family money or partner employment.
